actions.justification: Essential first step to classify the patient's hemodynamic profile (wet vs dry) — patient has lower extremity edema and dyspnea suggesting volume overload; this guides diuretic therapy decisions.
Critical to determine if patient is warm (adequate perfusion) or cold (poor perfusion/cardiogenic shock), which determines whether IV diuretics alone are appropriate vs. need for inotropes.
BNP/NT-proBNP is the key biomarker for confirming acute heart failure diagnosis and assessing severity of decompensation per AHA heart failure guidelines.

Chest X-ray is essential to confirm pulmonary edema, assess severity of congestion, and rule out alternative causes of dyspnea. This is a key diagnostic step in acute heart failure workup per AHA guidelines.

Patient presents with wet/warm heart failure (congestion with adequate perfusion — BP 132/82, SpO2 94%). IV furosemide is the first-line treatment for acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload per AHA guidelines. BNP and perfusion status already assessed support this intervention.

BMP (basic metabolic panel) is needed to assess renal function (creatinine, BUN), electrolytes (potassium, sodium), and establish baseline before initiating IV diuresis. Electrolyte abnormalities can be exacerbated by furosemide and must be monitored.
Echocardiogram is indicated to assess ejection fraction and wall motion abnormalities, which will guide further management of this patient's heart failure (HFrEF vs HFpEF distinction).
Troponin should be ordered to evaluate for underlying ACS as a precipitant of acute decompensated heart failure, especially given new onset presentation.
Cardiology consultation is appropriate for acute decompensated heart failure to guide ongoing management, medication optimization, and disposition planning.

Patient presents as WET and WARM (congested with adequate perfusion: BP 132/82, MAP 99, SpO2 94%). IV vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin) reduce preload and afterload, alleviating pulmonary congestion in warm heart failure. This is appropriate given adequate blood pressure and no signs of cardiogenic shock. IV diuresis has already been initiated; vasodilator therapy is a guideline-supported adjunct for symptomatic relief.

Patient has been assessed and treated for wet/warm heart failure with diuretics and vasodilators. With SpO2 at 94% and ongoing monitoring, if echo reveals reduced EF or perfusion status worsens toward a wet/cold picture (cardiogenic shock), inotropic support may be warranted. This is the only remaining available action and should be considered given the clinical trajectory and pending diagnostic results.
Mandatory action within 60-minute deadline. Obtaining a focused history is essential to characterize the onset, severity, and precipitants of this patient's acute heart failure presentation.
Mandatory action within 60-minute deadline. Physical examination to assess volume status (JVP, edema, crackles), perfusion, and hemodynamic profile is foundational in acute heart failure management.
Mandatory action within 60-minute deadline. ECG is needed to identify arrhythmias, ischemia, or conduction abnormalities that may be precipitating or complicating acute heart failure.
Mandatory action: assess renal function, electrolytes, and glucose which are critical for managing heart failure and guiding diuretic therapy.
Mandatory action: BNP/NT-proBNP is essential for confirming heart failure diagnosis and assessing severity of decompensation.
Mandatory action: chest X-ray to evaluate for pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly to guide management of acute heart failure.
Mandatory action - CBC to evaluate for anemia (which can exacerbate heart failure symptoms and dyspnea) and assess for infection or other hematologic abnormalities.
Mandatory action - TSH to rule out thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism) as a reversible cause or contributor to heart failure decompensation.

Patient has SpO2 94% with signs of congestion (edema, dyspnea). Hemodynamic profile assessment (wet/warm vs wet/cold) will guide further management including need for vasodilators, diuretic optimization, or inotropes.
LVEF assessment is critical to guide further HF management - determines if patient has HFrEF vs HFpEF, guiding evidence-based therapy selection (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i for HFrEF).

Patient presents with progressive dyspnea and lower extremity edema (wet profile) with SpO2 94%. IV diuretic has been started; additional diuretic therapy may be needed to achieve adequate decongestion and symptom relief.
Once LVEF is known, ICD candidacy should be evaluated if EF ≤35% despite optimal medical therapy, as per ACC/AHA HF guidelines for sudden cardiac death prevention.
Assessing NYHA functional class is essential to guide ongoing management, medication titration, and disposition planning for this heart failure patient with dyspnea and edema.

Patient's BP is 132/82 (MAP 99), indicating hypertension in the setting of acute heart failure. A vasodilator can reduce afterload, improve cardiac output, and relieve congestion in this wet/warm profile.
After LVEF assessment has been completed, evaluating CRT (cardiac resynchronization therapy) indication is appropriate per AHA HF guidelines to optimize long-term management.

Echo has been ordered; now assess for structural abnormalities (valvular disease, wall motion abnormalities) that may be contributing to heart failure and guide further management including GDMT optimization.

Patient is stable (warm and wet profile, SpO2 94%, adequate BP) and diuresis has been initiated. Assess current GDMT status and duration to optimize evidence-based therapy (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA) as per AHA heart failure guidelines.

With initial stabilization underway and cardiology consulted, early referral to cardiac rehabilitation should be planned as part of comprehensive heart failure management to improve functional capacity and outcomes.

Patient with heart failure requires confirmation of optimal guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) per AHA HF guidelines. Many initial assessments are complete and treatment has been initiated; now confirm all GDMT components are in place.

ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) is a cornerstone of GDMT for heart failure with reduced EF per AHA guidelines. Patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 132/82) and appropriate candidate for neurohormonal blockade.

Beta-blocker is essential GDMT for heart failure. Patient is hemodynamically stable and not in acute decompensation requiring IV agents. Oral beta-blocker (e.g., carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) should be initiated or confirmed per AHA HF guidelines. Note: IV beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute pulmonary edema per guideline.

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone) is indicated in HFrEF to reduce mortality and hospitalizations, and aids in diuresis. Patient has received IV diuretics; adding MRA supports ongoing decongestion and GDMT optimization.
If response to IV loop diuretic is inadequate, combining with a thiazide-type diuretic (metolazone) can overcome diuretic resistance and enhance decongestion in this congested heart failure patient.

Patient HR is 88 bpm; if the patient has HFrEF with LVEF ≤35% and remains symptomatic on maximally tolerated beta-blocker, ivabradine may be indicated per AHA/ACC guidelines to reduce heart failure hospitalization.

Patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 132/82, HR 88) after IV diuresis. Guidelines support continuing beta-blocker therapy in stable heart failure patients to maintain GDMT and reduce mortality, avoiding abrupt discontinuation.

Patient has hypertension (BP 132/82) with heart failure and congestion (WET/WARM profile). Vasodilators can reduce afterload and preload, complementing diuretic therapy to relieve symptoms and improve hemodynamics.

Patient has persistent dyspnea and edema at nearly 3 hours into management. If response to IV furosemide is inadequate, adding metolazone (thiazide-like diuretic) provides synergistic diuresis to overcome diuretic resistance.
Patient has SpO2 of 94% and RR of 20 with heart failure — continuous monitoring of vitals, SpO2, and rhythm is essential to detect deterioration and guide ongoing management.
Daily weights are a core component of acute heart failure management to assess response to diuretic therapy and guide fluid balance decisions.
If diuretic response is suboptimal (labs pending, congestion present), ultrafiltration may be considered as an alternative or adjunct strategy per heart failure guidelines for refractory congestion.

Patient has persistent congestion (dyspnea, edema, SpO2 94%) and has already received IV diuretic bolus. Continuous diuretic infusion may improve diuretic efficacy and symptom relief in refractory volume overload.

Patient remains symptomatic with SpO2 94%, RR 20, and ongoing congestion after >3 hours of management. Closer monitoring in ICU setting may be warranted to ensure adequate response to therapy and detect deterioration.
